title: How Dividends Are Taxed: Qualified vs Ordinary Dividends
content:
Dividends are payments that companies distribute to shareholders from their profits. While dividend income can be a great source of passive income, it's important to understand how the IRS taxes different types of dividends — because the tax rate can vary dramatically depending on the type of dividend and your income level.

## Two Types of Dividends

### 1. Qualified Dividends
Qualified dividends are taxed at the lower long-term capital gains rates (0%, 15%, or 20% depending on your income bracket in 2024). To be "qualified," a dividend must meet specific IRS requirements:

- **The stock must be from a U.S. corporation** or a qualified foreign corporation (most foreign stocks traded on U.S. exchanges qualify).
- **Holding period requirement**: You must have held the stock for more than 60 days during the 121-day period that begins 60 days before the ex-dividend date. In practice, this means buy-and-hold investors almost always meet this requirement, while frequent traders may not.

### 2. Ordinary (Non-Qualified) Dividends
Ordinary dividends do not meet the qualified dividend criteria and are taxed as ordinary income at your marginal tax rate — which can be as high as 37% in 2024. Sources of ordinary dividends typically include:
- Dividends from money market funds
- Dividends paid on employee stock options
- Dividends from certain foreign corporations
- Short-term capital gain distributions from mutual funds
- **REIT dividends** (mostly ordinary, see below)

## 2024 Qualified Dividend Tax Rates

| Taxable Income (Single) | Qualified Dividend Rate |
|---|---|
| Up to $47,025 | 0% |
| $47,026 – $518,900 | 15% |
| Above $518,900 | 20% |

High earners may also owe the 3.8% Net Investment Income Tax (NIIT) on top of the 20% rate, bringing the effective top rate to 23.8%.

## REIT Dividends: A Special Case

Real Estate Investment Trusts (REITs) are required by law to distribute at least 90% of their taxable income to shareholders as dividends. However, most REIT dividends are classified as **ordinary dividends**, not qualified dividends, because REITs don't pay corporate income tax at the entity level. This means REIT dividends are taxed at your full ordinary income rate.

The good news: Under the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA), investors may be eligible for the **20% qualified business income (QBI) deduction** on REIT dividends, effectively reducing the tax rate by up to 20% of the dividend amount. However, the TCJA provisions are set to expire after 2025, so this may change.

**REIT tax tip:** Because of their high ordinary dividend taxes, REITs are often best held in tax-advantaged accounts (IRA, 401k) rather than taxable brokerage accounts.

## How to Minimize Dividend Taxes

### 1. Hold Dividend-Paying Stocks in Tax-Advantaged Accounts
Place high-dividend investments (especially REITs, bond funds, and high-yield dividend stocks) inside your 401(k) or IRA, where dividends can compound without annual taxation.

### 2. Use Tax-Efficient Funds in Taxable Accounts
In taxable accounts, favor growth-oriented index funds that pay little or no dividends (e.g., growth stock ETFs), or broad market index funds that focus on qualified dividend payers.

### 3. Satisfy Holding Periods
Make sure you hold dividend-paying stocks long enough to qualify for the lower qualified dividend rate. This is usually not an issue for long-term investors.

### 4. Manage Your Tax Bracket
If your income falls below the 0% qualified dividend threshold ($47,025 for single filers in 2024), you owe zero federal tax on qualified dividends. This can be valuable for retirees or those with flexible income.

### 5. Consider Dividend Reinvestment Plans (DRIPs)
DRIPs automatically reinvest dividends into more shares. Keep careful records — each reinvested dividend is a taxable event and raises your cost basis, which matters when you eventually sell.

## Reporting Dividends on Your Tax Return

Brokerages report dividends on **Form 1099-DIV** each year. Box 1a shows total ordinary dividends; Box 1b shows the qualified dividend subset. Qualified dividends are reported on Schedule B and taxed at capital gains rates on Form 1040.
